entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Love does not judge of resentment, nor resentment of love.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: In The Theory of Moral Sentiments, Smith argues that no single passion has the right to judge another; only conscience can stand above them.

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Nothing but exemplary morals can give dignity to a man of small fortune.
entries.work: An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations
entries.context: In The Wealth of Nations, Smith observes that clergy on modest incomes earn respect only through the example of their conduct.

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: There is something agreeable even in the weakness of friendship and humanity.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, on why even excessive tenderness and generosity are regarded kindly rather than with aversion.

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Our sympathy with sorrow, though not more real, has been more taken notice of than our sympathy with joy.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments opens its discussion of sympathy by noting that we attend more to shared grief than to shared happiness.

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: It is evident, however, that we are anxious about our own beauty and deformity only on account of its effect upon others.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, arguing that concern for how we look, and for how we behave, exists only because other people see us.

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Nothing tends so much to corrupt mankind as dependency, while independency still increases the honesty of the people.
entries.work: Lectures on Justice, Police, Revenue and Arms
entries.context: From student notes of Smith's Glasgow lectures on law and government, on why dependence on patrons corrupts people more than any police can correct.

entries.name: Adam Smith
entries.en: Nothing is so soon forgot as pain.
entries.work: The Theory of Moral Sentiments
entries.context: The Theory of Moral Sentiments, explaining why we sympathise little with bodily pain: once it has passed, it is hardly remembered.

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: The man who disassociates his ambition, however disinterested, from the coöperation of his fellows, always takes this risk of ultimate failure.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: In Democracy and Social Ethics, Addams writes about reformers who act alone rather than alongside the people they mean to help.

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: It is not comfortable to outrage the conventions of those among whom we live, and, if our social life be a narrow one, it is still more difficult.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics, on the pressure poor families feel to follow their neighbours' customs even when outsiders call them wasteful.

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: It is impossible to bring about the higher development by any self-assertion or breaking away of the individual will.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics, on the friction between daughters and families: growth comes through the family's claims, not by breaking from them.

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: There is no doubt that most of the misunderstandings of life are due to partial intelligence, because our experiences have been so unlike that we cannot comprehend each other.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics argues that people misjudge each other because their experiences of life have been so different.

entries.name: Jane Addams
entries.en: We are constantly underestimating the amount of sentiment among simple people.
entries.work: Democracy and Social Ethics
entries.context: Democracy and Social Ethics, written from Hull-House in Chicago, on the feeling for memory and old age in the songs immigrant neighbours loved.

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: Virtue then is in a sense a mean state, since it certainly has an aptitude for aiming at the mean.
entries.work: The Nicomachean Ethics
entries.context: In the Nicomachean Ethics, Aristotle sets out his doctrine that virtue lies in a mean between excess and deficiency.

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: Character is that which reveals moral purpose, showing what kind of things a man chooses or avoids.
entries.work: Poetics
entries.context: The Poetics, on character in tragedy: a dramatic character shows itself in what a person chooses and what they avoid.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: Love is impatient and unless to her is given what is loved, grief has no limit.
entries.work: The Soliloquies of St. Augustine
entries.context: The Soliloquies, a dialogue between Augustine and Reason; here Augustine speaks as they turn to the second book.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: No man loves what he endures, though he love to endure.
entries.work: The Confessions of Saint Augustine
entries.context: In the Confessions, Augustine reflects that troubles are to be endured, not loved, even by someone who takes pride in bearing them.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: It is the decided opinion of all who use their brains, that all men desire to be happy.
entries.work: The City of God
entries.locator: OF PROVIDING MEN WITH ETERNAL BLESSEDNESS, BOOK I
entries.context: The City of God opens a long inquiry into happiness with a point Augustine takes as agreed by everyone.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: Nature is to be judged by capacity, education by knowledge, practice by its fruit.
entries.work: The City of God
entries.locator: OF THE BOOK OF GENESIS, BOOK I
entries.context: The City of God, on the three things every craftsman needs, which Augustine borrows to describe the parts of philosophy.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: Every where the greater joy is ushered in by the greater pain.
entries.work: The Confessions of Saint Augustine
entries.context: In the Confessions, Augustine wonders why recovering what was lost moves us more than never losing it.

entries.name: Augustine of Hippo
entries.en: The mind commands the mind, its own self, to will, and yet it doth not.
entries.work: The Confessions of Saint Augustine
entries.context: The Confessions, Book VIII: Augustine puzzling over a will divided against itself in the months before his conversion.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Seek not proud riches, but such as thou mayest get justly, use soberly, distribute cheerfully, and leave contentedly.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Riches", advice on how to hold wealth without contempt and without greed.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Let not a man force a habit upon himself, with a perpetual continuance, but with some intermission.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Nature in Men", on changing your habits by practice with pauses rather than by unbroken strain.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: A wise man will make more opportunities, than he finds.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Ceremonies and Respects", on manners, timing and opportunity.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: There is surely no greater wisdom, than well to time the beginnings, and onsets, of things.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Delays", on timing: dangers handled early are smaller.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Wisdom for a man's self is, in many branches thereof, a depraved thing.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: The opening line of Bacon's essay "Of Wisdom for a Man's Self", on the kind of cleverness that serves only oneself.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Anger must be limited and confined, both in race and in time.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Anger": not to abolish anger, but to limit how far it goes and how long it lasts.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: Whosoever is out of patience, is out of possession of his soul.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Anger", echoing the scriptural counsel to possess one's soul in patience.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: He that builds a fair house, upon an ill seat, committeth himself to prison.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Building", about the siting of actual houses; the line reads as a figure, but Bacon meant it literally.

entries.name: Francis Bacon
entries.en: He that is too much in anything, so that he giveth another occasion of satiety, maketh himself cheap.
entries.work: The Essays or Counsels, Civil and Moral
entries.context: From Bacon's essay "Of Ceremonies and Respects", on keeping a little reserve in company.

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Every motive, in the final analysis, is the perspective of a pleasure to be procured, or of a pain to be avoided.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, an English version of Bentham's work edited by Dumont, arguing that motives are neither good nor bad in themselves.

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Every new and important truth must of necessity have many enemies, for the single reason that it is new and important.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, arguing against censorship of the press.

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Love which descends has more force than love which ascends.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, on family duties: the love of parents for children is stronger than children's gratitude to parents.

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: Nothing is more common than to authorize under one name what would be odious under another.
entries.work: The Theory of Legislation
entries.context: The Theory of Legislation, on how the same act is excused when it is given a different name.

entries.name: Jeremy Bentham
entries.en: It is only in the absence of interest that experience can hope to be regarded, or reason heard.
entries.work: The Book of Fallacies
entries.context: The Book of Fallacies, Bentham's catalogue of bad political arguments, on why self-interested people cannot weigh experience fairly.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: All that is serious in life comes from our freedom.
entries.work: Laughter: An Essay on the Meaning of the Comic
entries.locator: OF WORDS WE GENERALLY FIND TWO
entries.context: Laughter, Bergson's essay on the comic, explaining why tragedy and serious life belong to freedom while comedy belongs to automatism.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: To act is to re-adapt oneself.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, on the intellect as a tool for action: to act is to keep adjusting to a changing situation.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: The more we study the nature of time, the more we shall comprehend that duration means invention, the creation of forms, the continual elaboration of the absolutely new.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, Bergson's central claim that time as lived is continual invention rather than repetition.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: Our intellect has been cast in the mold of action.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, arguing that we first think in order to act, so the intellect is shaped for practical use.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: We must recognize that all is not coherent in nature.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, allowing that accident and incoherence are real in the history of life.

entries.name: Henri Bergson
entries.en: Nature is more and better than a plan in course of realization.
entries.work: Creative Evolution
entries.context: Creative Evolution, arguing that life is not the carrying out of a plan fixed in advance.

entries.name: George Berkeley
entries.en: The more doubt the more room there is for faith, a sceptic of all men having the least right to demand evidence.
entries.work: Alciphron; or, The Minute Philosopher
entries.context: Alciphron, Berkeley's dialogue against the freethinkers; here his spokesman argues that doubting everything is no ground for refusing faith.

entries.name: Boethius
entries.en: Never will fortune make thine that which the nature of things has excluded from thy ownership.
entries.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
entries.context: The Consolation of Philosophy, written in prison; Philosophy tells the grieving Boethius that fortune's gifts were never his to keep.

entries.name: Boethius
entries.en: Nature is content with few things, and with a very little of these.
entries.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
entries.context: The Consolation of Philosophy: Philosophy argues that what nature truly needs is small, and fortune's extras add nothing.

entries.name: Boethius
entries.en: Look upon the infinitude, the solidity, the swift motion, of the heavens, and for once cease to admire things mean and worthless.
entries.work: The Consolation of Philosophy
entries.context: The Consolation of Philosophy: Philosophy turns Boethius from bodily goods to the order of the heavens.

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: Love, when real, ever desires light, in order to attain its ends.
entries.work: A General View of Positivism
entries.context: A General View of Positivism, Comte's summary of his system, arguing that true feeling helps thought rather than clouding it.

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: Love cannot be deep unless it remains constant to a fixed object.
entries.work: A General View of Positivism
entries.context: A General View of Positivism, Comte's case for constancy in love and marriage.

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: Our life is really destined to be a compound of resignation and action.
entries.work: The Catechism of Positive Religion
entries.context: The Catechism of Positivism, a dialogue setting out Comte's "religion of humanity"; here the priest speaks, Comte's own spokesman.

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: All practical work requires as the first condition of its success that each one who co-operates should be honest, intelligent, and courageous.
entries.work: The Catechism of Positive Religion
entries.context: The Catechism of Positivism, on the qualities any shared work depends on.

entries.name: Auguste Comte
entries.en: The best workmen, like the best philosophers, will soon cease to feel envy for greatness, laden, as it always must be, with heavy responsibilities.
entries.work: A General View of Positivism
entries.context: A General View of Positivism, imagining workers in a future society freed from envy of those who hold power.

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: He who wishes truth to be generated without error wishes for the son without the father.

entries.name: Benedetto Croce

entries.name: Benedetto Croce
entries.en: Love passes, but generates other beings, who will love.

entries.context: Human Nature and Conduct, on rest and recovery coming through useful work rather than escape from it.

entries.name: John Dewey

entries.work: Human Nature and Conduct: An Introduction to Social Psychology

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: To work is not only a right, it is a duty.

entries.en: Let no one tremble in fear of losing precious things.

entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, reassuring readers that reforming the home will not destroy what is precious in it.

entries.en: Learn what we may of art and science, the art of living, the science of living is not yet known to us.
entries.work: The Home: Its Work and Influence
entries.context: The Home: Its Work and Influence, on how little we know about living well, even with modern science.

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman
entries.en: Love has to pass muster in results, as well as intentions.

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

entries.name: Charlotte Perkins Gilman

entries.name: William Godwin

entries.locator: OF THE ISFLVEKCE OF CLIMATE, Book IV
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice: innocence is not virtue, since virtue takes thought and effort for the general good.

entries.name: William Godwin

entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, on how courts and luxury corrupt those who live around them.

entries.name: William Godwin

entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, on spreading knowledge, not passing laws, as the way to reform a society.

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: Nothing can be more unworthy, than a propensity to take refuge in indolence and neutrality, simply because we have not the courage to encounter the consequences of ingenuousness and sincerity.

entries.locator: OF THE MODES OF DECIDING A QUESTION ON THE, Book VIII
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, against staying neutral out of fear of what honesty will cost.

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: Nothing perhaps can put a stop to the advances of mind but oppression.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, on thought begetting thought when people are free and at ease.

entries.name: William Godwin
entries.en: He who has tasted the pleasures of refinement and knowledge, will not relapse into ignorance.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, and Its Influence on Morals and Happiness
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning Political Justice, arguing that the love of knowledge would outlast the end of great wealth.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel

entries.work: The Logic of Hegel

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel
entries.en: True thoughts and scientific insight can only be won by the labour of the notion.
entries.work: The Phenomenology of Mind
entries.context: The Preface to the Phenomenology of Mind, against relying on flashes of feeling instead of the slow work of thinking.

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: Time, and industry, produce every day new knowledge.

entries.context: Leviathan, answering those who think a lasting political order is impossible because none has yet been built.

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: Courage may be virtue, when the daring is extreme, if the cause be good, and extreme fear no vice when the danger is extreme.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 04 (of 11)
entries.context: Hobbes rejecting Aristotle's doctrine of the mean: courage can be a virtue even at its extreme, if the cause is good.

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: It is no inconstancy in a man to love or to hate as the object is changed.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 05 (of 11)
entries.context: From Hobbes's controversy on liberty and necessity: changing one's feelings toward something that has changed is not inconstancy.

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: Nature dictates the seeking after peace.

entries.context: From Hobbes's list of the laws of nature, which begins with the duty to seek peace.

entries.name: Thomas Hobbes
entries.en: There is nothing in learning more difficult than to determine the signification of words.
entries.work: The English works of Thomas Hobbes of Malmesbury, Volume 04 (of 11)
entries.context: From Hobbes's dispute with Bishop Bramhall, on the difficulty of fixing what words mean.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Pain and pleasure, grief and joy, passions and sensations succeed each other, and never all exist at the same time.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, Hume's argument that no single feeling stays with us constantly enough to be the self.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: No man is absolutely indifferent to the happiness and misery of others.
entries.work: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals
entries.context: An Enquiry Concerning the Principles of Morals, on sympathy as a basic and universal principle.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Every pleasure languishes when enjoyed a-part from company, and every pain becomes more cruel and intolerable.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.locator: OF THE LATTER A SEPARATE UNEASINESS
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, on how much our feelings depend on the company of others.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Courage and ambition, when not regulated by benevolence, are fit only to make a tyrant and public robber.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.locator: OF OUR OWN HAPPINESS, AND GIVES US PLEASURE
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, on benevolence as the virtue that steers all the others.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Nothing is more dangerous to reason than the flights of the imagination, and nothing has been the occasion of more mistakes among philosophers.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, near the end of Book I, on imagination as the source of philosophers' errors.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Nothing causes any sentiment to have a greater influence upon us than custom, or turns our imagination more strongly to any object.
entries.work: A Treatise of Human Nature
entries.context: A Treatise of Human Nature, on how long habit makes a government seem legitimate.

entries.name: David Hume
entries.en: Nothing is pure and entirely of a piece.
entries.work: The Natural History of Religion
entries.context: The Natural History of Religion, near its close: good and ill are mixed in every human condition.

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: Happiness alone is, in the view of reason, far from being the complete good.
entries.work: Critique of Pure Reason (Meiklejohn)
entries.translator: Meiklejohn, J. M. D. (John Miller Dow) (d. 1902)
entries.context: The Critique of Pure Reason, in its discussion of the highest good: happiness counts only when it is joined with deserving it.

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: We must be able to will that a maxim of our action should be a universal law.
entries.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
entries.context: The Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, stating Kant's test for any moral rule.

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: All men attribute to themselves freedom of will.
entries.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
entries.context: The Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals, in its closing discussion of the limits of practical philosophy.

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: All ignorance is either ignorance of things or of the limits of knowledge.
entries.work: Critique of Pure Reason (Meiklejohn)
entries.translator: Meiklejohn, J. M. D. (John Miller Dow) (d. 1902)
entries.context: The Critique of Pure Reason, on two kinds of ignorance and why knowing the limits of knowledge matters.

entries.name: Immanuel Kant
entries.en: Nothing can possibly be conceived in the world, or even out of it, which can be called good, without qualification, except a good will.
entries.work: Fundamental Principles of the Metaphysic of Morals
entries.context: The first line of the first section of Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysic of Morals.

entries.name: Peter Kropotkin
entries.en: There are not many joys in human life equal to the joy of the sudden birth of a generalization, illuminating the mind after a long period of patient research.
entries.work: Memoirs of a Revolutionist
entries.context: Memoirs of a Revolutionist, Kropotkin recalling the years of his geographical research.

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: No man can be wholly ignorant of what he does when he thinks.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.locator: OF THE BODY, AS MAKES IT BE TAKEN NOTICE OF, CHAPTER IV
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, on how the mind cannot help having some notion of its own workings.

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: He that hath names without ideas, wants meaning in his words, and speaks only empty sounds.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.locator: OF THINGS WHICH THEY DO OR CAN BY NO MEANS, BOOK III
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book III, on the abuse of words.

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: He that uses his words loosely and unsteadily will either be not minded or not understood.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.locator: OF THINGS WHICH THEY DO OR CAN BY NO MEANS, BOOK III
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, Book III, on careless use of words.

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: He that knows anything, knows this, in the first place, that he need not seek long for instances of his ignorance.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, on how quickly anyone runs into the limits of what they know.

entries.name: John Locke
entries.en: The mind thinks in proportion to the matter it gets from experience to think about.
entries.work: An Essay Concerning Humane Understanding
entries.context: An Essay Concerning Human Understanding, arguing that thinking grows with experience, as you can see in a child.

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: Every one admits how praiseworthy it is in a prince to keep faith, and to live with integrity and not with craft.
entries.work: The Prince
entries.locator: OF THE ART OF WAR, CHAPTER XVIII
entries.context: The opening of chapter XVIII of The Prince, on whether a ruler should keep his word; the chapter goes on to argue that successful princes often have not.

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: He who believes that new benefits will cause great personages to forget old injuries is deceived.
entries.work: The Prince
entries.locator: OF OTHERS OR BY GOOD FORTUNE, CHAPTER VII
entries.context: The Prince, on Cesare Borgia's fatal mistake of trusting an old enemy he had newly favoured.

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: Nature breedeth few stronge menne, the industrie and the exercise maketh manie.
entries.work: The Art of War
entries.context: The Art of War, in its 1560 English translation, from a list of military maxims on training.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, private notes to himself written in Greek, here in Casaubon's seventeenth-century English.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: The best kind of revenge is, not to become like unto them.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on answering people who wrong you.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let thy mind penetrate both into the effects, and into the causes.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, from a run of short reminders to himself.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let not thy mind wander up and down, and heap together in her thoughts the many troubles and grievous calamities which thou art as subject unto as any other.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on not letting imagined future troubles crowd in at once.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, a rule for acting.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Be neither a great talker, nor a great undertaker.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, from a passage on plain speech and steady conduct.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on how much of being wronged lies in our opinion of it.

entries.name: Marcus Aurelius
entries.en: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way.
entries.work: The Meditations of the Emperor Marcus Aurelius Antoninus
entries.context: The Meditations, on taking the shortest way, which is the way of nature.

entries.name: Karl Marx
entries.en: The more or less extensive application of division of labour depends on length of purse, not on greatness of genius.
entries.work: Capital: A Critique of Political Economy, Volume I
entries.context: Capital, Volume I, in a footnote mocking the idea that the division of labour was a capitalist's stroke of genius.

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: It is not necessary for keeping up our conviction that we must die, that we should be always brooding over death.
entries.work: Three Essays on Religion: Nature, The Utility of Religion, and Theism
entries.context: Three Essays on Religion, in the essay "Theism", on thinking about death no more than we need to.

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: He who does anything because it is the custom, makes no choice.
entries.work: On Liberty
entries.context: On Liberty, chapter III, on individuality: our faculties grow only when we use them to choose.

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: Nothing has so steadying an influence as working against pressure.
entries.work: Considerations on Representative Government
entries.context: Considerations on Representative Government, on the value of having to defend one's views against opposition.

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: Whoever is anxious that a discussion should go to the bottom of the subject, must rejoice to see the opposite side of the question worthily represented.
entries.work: A System of Logic, Ratiocinative and Inductive
entries.context: A System of Logic, welcoming the strongest statement of the view Mill was arguing against.

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: No one pretends that actions should be as free as opinions.
entries.work: On Liberty
entries.context: On Liberty, chapter III, which opens by limiting liberty of action more than liberty of opinion.

entries.name: John Stuart Mill
entries.en: There is no natural connection between strong impulses and a weak conscience.
entries.work: On Liberty
entries.context: On Liberty, chapter III, arguing that people go wrong not because their desires are strong but because their consciences are weak.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Men of principle are sure to be bold, but those who are bold may not always be men of principle.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects of Confucius, sayings recorded by his followers, here in James Legge's translation; this is from Book XIV.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, attributed to Laozi, here in James Legge's translation; chapter 9.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: There is no calamity greater than lightly engaging in war.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 69, on the conduct of war.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: It is the Way of Heaven to diminish superabundance, and to supplement deficiency.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 77, comparing the Way of Heaven with the way of man.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: Every one in the world knows that the soft overcomes the hard, and the weak the strong, but no one is able to carry it out in practice.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 78, on water, softness and strength.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 15, on the old masters of the Way and muddy water settling.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: All difficult things in the world are sure to arise from a previous state in which they were easy, and all great things from one in which they were small.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 63, on attending to things while they are still small.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: He who loves others is always loved by them, and he who respects others is always respected by them.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF BEING CAREFUL WHOM WE MAKE FRIENDS OF, chapter XXIII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, in James Legge's translation, on benevolence and propriety.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: There is no greater delight than to be conscious of sincerity on self-examination.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VII, on looking within: "All things are already complete in us."

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: Never has a man who has bent himself been able to make others straight.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book III, on refusing to bend one's principles to win a ruler's favour.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: He who behaves shabbily to those whom he ought to treat well will behave shabbily to all.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF TRUTH IN THOSE WHOM HE TAUGHT, Book IX
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VII, from a chapter of short sayings on character.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: It is only the great man who can correct what is wrong in the ruler's mind.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book IV, on the counsellor's real task.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: Men constantly err, but are afterwards able to reform.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF SEVERAL EMINENT WORTHIES OF FORMER TIMES, Book VII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VI, on how hardship and mistakes lead people to change.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: He who will not give himself leisure to be thirsty can never find the true pleasure of drinking.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, in Charles Cotton's translation, on how pleasure dulls with constant use.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Fear springs sometimes as much from want of judgment as from want of courage.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, Montaigne recalling that he never lost his judgment in danger.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: There is no desire more natural than that of knowledge.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: The opening line of Montaigne's final essay, "Of Experience".

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Nothing can be a grievance that is but once.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.locator: OF OUR HAPPINESS TILL AFTER DEATH
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, on not fearing death too long, since it happens only once.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Nothing is so distasteful and clogging as abundance.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, on how excess kills appetite and restraint sharpens pleasure.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: Whoever will be cured of ignorance must confess it.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, on scholars who would rather appear learned than admit what they do not understand.

entries.name: Michel de Montaigne
entries.en: We should rather examine, who is better learned, than who is more learned.
entries.work: The Essays of Michel de Montaigne
entries.locator: OF CUSTOM, AND THAT WE SHOULD NOT EASILY
entries.context: Montaigne's Essays, in "Of Pedantry", criticising education that fills the memory but does not improve the person.

entries.name: Friedrich Nietzsche
entries.en: All great noise causes one to place happiness in the calm and the distance.
entries.work: The Joyful Wisdom ("La Gaya Scienza")
entries.translator: Thomas Common (prose; verse by Paul V. Cohn)
entries.context: The Joyful Wisdom (The Gay Science), on longing for calm in the middle of noise.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: He who should find the secret of rejoicing in good without being troubled at its contrary evil, would have hit the mark.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts (Pensées), notes for an unfinished defence of Christianity, on why we cannot enjoy any good without fearing its loss.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: Time heals all pain and misunderstanding, because we change and are no longer the same persons.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on time changing both the person who gave offence and the person who took it.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: All the efforts of violence cannot weaken truth, and only serve to give it fresh vigor.
entries.work: The Provincial Letters
entries.context: The Provincial Letters, Pascal's satirical letters against the Jesuits; from the twelfth, on the war between violence and truth.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: It is not shameful to man to yield to pain, and it is shameful to yield to pleasure.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on the difference between yielding to pain and yielding to pleasure.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: It is false piety to keep peace to the prejudice of the truth.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on the balance between loving truth and keeping charity.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: Nothing fortifies scepticism more than that there are some who are not sceptics.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, a fragment on scepticism.

entries.name: Blaise Pascal
entries.en: Whoever stops draws attention to the onward movement of others, as does a fixed point.
entries.work: The Thoughts of Blaise Pascal
entries.context: Pascal's Thoughts, on how we notice that others are moving only when someone stands still.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: Let every man, then, freely strive for the prize of virtue, and let there be no envy.
entries.work: Laws
entries.context: Plato's Laws, his longest dialogue; the Athenian Stranger speaks, on rivalry in virtue without envy.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: Let parents, then, bequeath to their children not a heap of riches, but the spirit of reverence.
entries.work: Laws
entries.context: Plato's Laws: the Athenian Stranger on what parents should leave their children.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: It is an intimation that what has happened to me is a good, and that those of us who think that death is an evil are in error.
entries.work: Apology
entries.context: Plato's Apology, Socrates' defence speech at his trial, after the verdict of death.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: Our statement, then, is true, that the very rich are not good, and, if they are not good, they are not happy.
entries.work: Laws
entries.context: Plato's Laws: the Athenian Stranger on why great wealth and goodness rarely go together.

entries.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
entries.en: He who prefers truth to fame, may hope to prefer it to life itself.
entries.work: Eloisa
entries.context: From Rousseau's preface to Julie, or the New Eloisa, his novel in letters, defending its publication.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: The best part of wealth is to have worthy heirs, and mind can be transmitted only to a kindred mind.
entries.work: The Life of Reason, Volume One: Reason in Common Sense
entries.context: The Life of Reason, Volume One, on why we want others to share and carry on what we care about.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Love makes us poets, and the approach of death should make us philosophers.
entries.work: The Sense of Beauty: Being the Outlines of Aesthetic Theory
entries.context: The Sense of Beauty, on the eloquence of the dying in tragedy.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Love is very penetrating, but it penetrates to possibilities rather than to facts.
entries.work: Character and Opinion in the United States
entries.context: Character and Opinion in the United States, from Santayana's portrait of his teacher William James.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Never was the human mind master of so many facts and sure of so few principles.
entries.work: Character and Opinion in the United States
entries.context: Character and Opinion in the United States, on the open, unsettled state of modern thought.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Nothing so much enhances a good as to make sacrifices for it.
entries.work: The Sense of Beauty: Being the Outlines of Aesthetic Theory
entries.context: The Sense of Beauty, on how what people suffer for becomes dear to them.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Great empty spaces bring a sort of freedom to both soul and body.
entries.work: Character and Opinion in the United States
entries.context: Character and Opinion in the United States, on the American landscape and the American temper.

entries.name: George Santayana
entries.en: Life begins to have some value and continuity so soon as there is something definite that lives and something definite to live for.
entries.work: The Life of Reason, Volume One: Reason in Common Sense
entries.context: The Life of Reason, Volume One, on the moment life acquires direction.

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.en: Love of praise has in large measure served in place of love of rectitude.
entries.work: The Principles of Ethics
entries.context: The Principles of Ethics, on how the wish for reputation has stood in for real moral feeling.

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.en: Do not expect from a child any great amount of moral goodness.
entries.work: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical
entries.context: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical, Spencer's advice to parents on moral training.

entries.name: Herbert Spencer
entries.en: Do not regret the exhibition of considerable self-will on the part of your children.
entries.work: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical
entries.context: Education: Intellectual, Moral, and Physical, on wilfulness in children as a sign of growing independence.

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: Love is pleasure, accompanied by the idea of an external cause.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part III, from the definitions of the emotions.

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: He who is led by fear, and does good in order to escape evil, is not led by reason.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on acting from reason rather than fear.

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: Love and desire may be excessive.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on when pleasure and desire become harmful.

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: The mind's absolute virtue is therefore to understand.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on understanding as the mind's own virtue.

entries.name: Baruch Spinoza
entries.en: The highest good of those who follow virtue is common to all, and therefore all can equally rejoice therein.
entries.work: Ethics
entries.translator: Elwes, R. H. M. (Robert Harvey Monro) (d. 1892)
entries.context: Spinoza's Ethics, Part IV, on the highest good, which is lessened by no one else having it too.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: He who is only a traveller learns things at second-hand and by the halves, and is poor authority.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, on the difference between a traveller's knowledge and that of people who live in a place.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Men do not fail commonly for want of knowledge, but for want of prudence to give wisdom the preference.
entries.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
entries.context: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, Thoreau's account of a boat trip with his brother, on prudence and wisdom.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Nature is as well adapted to our weakness as to our strength.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, in "Economy", on how much anxious care we could safely give up.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Take your time, and set about some free labor.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, in "Economy", on doing good without making a business of it.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Let your life be a counter friction to stop the machine.
entries.work: On the Duty of Civil Disobedience
entries.context: Civil Disobedience, on refusing to lend oneself to an injustice one condemns.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Nothing can rightly compel a simple and brave man to a vulgar sadness.
entries.work: Walden; or, Life in the Woods
entries.context: Walden, in "Solitude", on how nature keeps off melancholy.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: There are moments when all anxiety and stated toil are becalmed in the infinite leisure and repose of nature.
entries.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
entries.context: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, on a midday rest on the river.

entries.name: Henry David Thoreau
entries.en: Our life without love is like coke and ashes.
entries.work: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers
entries.context: A Week on the Concord and Merrimack Rivers, in a long passage on friendship.

entries.name: William James
entries.en: Truth must bring clear thoughts, as well as clear the way to action.
entries.work: The Meaning of Truth
entries.context: The Meaning of Truth, William James defending pragmatism's account of truth against its critics.

entries.name: William James
entries.en: There is the strangest lightness about the heart when one's nothingness in a particular line is once accepted in good faith.
entries.work: The Principles of Psychology, Volume 1 (of 2)
entries.context: The Principles of Psychology, in the chapter on the self, on the relief of giving up a pretension.

entries.name: William James
entries.en: We must care more for our honor, our friends, our human ties, than for a sound skin or wealth.
entries.work: The Principles of Psychology, Volume 1 (of 2)
entries.context: The Principles of Psychology, on how we rank the parts of the self: social and spiritual above material.

entries.name: William James
entries.en: He who loves to balance nice doubts need be in no hurry to decide the point.
entries.work: The Principles of Psychology, Volume 2 (of 2)
entries.context: The Principles of Psychology, Volume II, on questions that introspection alone cannot settle.

entries.name: William James
entries.en: The best repentance is to up and act for righteousness, and forget that you ever had relations with sin.
entries.work: The Varieties of Religious Experience: A Study in Human Nature
entries.context: The Varieties of Religious Experience, where James describes the "healthy-minded" religious temper; the sentence sets out that view, which James examines rather than simply endorses.

entries.name: William James
entries.en: There is nothing to make one indignant in the mere fact that life is hard, that men should toil and suffer pain.
entries.work: Memories and Studies
entries.context: From "The Moral Equivalent of War", James's essay arguing for a peaceful outlet for martial virtues.

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Always determine, on every occasion, to speak the truth, and you will never be at a loss for words.
entries.work: Original Stories from Real Life
entries.context: Original Stories from Real Life, Wollstonecraft's book for children; the teacher Mrs Mason speaks to her pupils.

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Love gilds all the prospects of life, and though it cannot always exclude apathy, it makes many cares appear trifling.
entries.work: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
entries.locator: OF FEMALES, FASHIONABLY EDUCATED, AND LEFT
entries.context: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, Wollstonecraft's first book, on taking the joys that cost nothing in innocence.

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Love and compassion are the most delightful feelings of the soul, and to exert them to all that breathe is the wish of the benevolent heart.
entries.work: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters
entries.locator: OF FEMALES, FASHIONABLY EDUCATED, AND LEFT
entries.context: Thoughts on the Education of Daughters, on forbearance and kindness.

entries.name: Mary Wollstonecraft
entries.en: Let people but watch their own hearts, and act rightly as far as they can judge, and they may patiently wait till the opinion of the world comes round.
entries.work: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman
entries.context: A Vindication of the Rights of Woman, on acting rightly without anxiety about appearances.

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: Joy and anger, sorrow and happiness, caution and remorse, come upon us by turns, with ever-changing mood.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu (the Zhuangzi), in Herbert Giles's 1889 translation; from chapter II, on the endless round of moods.

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: There is no sorrow to be compared with the death of the mind.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, in a story where the character Confucius speaks to his disciple Yen Hui; Zhuangzi often puts his own ideas in Confucius's mouth.

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: The best language is that which is not spoken, the best form of action is that which is without deeds.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, from a passage on knowledge and its limits.

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: Those who make wealth their all in all, cannot bear loss of money.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, on how what we make everything of becomes what we cannot bear to lose.

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: Life must bring us from somewhere, and death must carry us back.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, on life and death as one ceaseless process.

entries.name: Zhuangzi
entries.en: There is nothing more fatal than intentional virtue, when the mind looks outwards.
entries.work: Chuang Tzu: Mystic, Moralist, and Social Reformer
entries.context: Chuang Tzu, in a passage on how virtue aimed at outward show destroys the power to look within.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: If a man keeps cherishing his old knowledge, so as continually to be acquiring new, he may be a teacher of others.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects of Confucius, Book II, chapter 11, in James Legge's translation.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Learning without thought is labour lost; thought without learning is perilous.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book II, chapter 15, on learning and thinking.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: If a man in the morning hear the right way, he may die in the evening without regret.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 8, on hearing the Way.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: When we see men of worth, we should think of equalling them; when we see men of a contrary character, we should turn inwards and examine ourselves.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 17, on learning from others' examples.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: The superior man wishes to be slow in his speech and earnest in his conduct.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 24, on the "superior man" (junzi), Confucius's ideal of the cultivated person.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Virtue is not left to stand alone. He who practises it will have neighbors.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book IV, chapter 25.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: They who know the truth are not equal to those who love it, and they who love it are not equal to those who delight in it.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VI, chapter 18, on degrees of devotion to the truth.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: When I walk along with two others, they may serve me as my teachers.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VII, chapter 21; it goes on, "I will select their good qualities and follow them, their bad qualities and avoid them."

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Is virtue a thing remote? I wish to be virtuous, and lo! virtue is at hand.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VII, chapter 29.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: The superior man is satisfied and composed; the mean man is always full of distress.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VII, chapter 36, contrasting the superior man with the "mean man" (xiaoren).

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: Learn as if you could not reach your object, and were always fearing also lest you should lose it.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book VIII, chapter 17, on the attitude of a learner.

entries.name: Confucius
entries.en: When you have faults, do not fear to abandon them.
entries.work: The Analects of Confucius
entries.context: The Analects, Book I, chapter 8, from a saying on the conduct of the scholar.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 33, in James Legge's translation.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: He who is satisfied with his lot is rich
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 33; it continues, "he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will."

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: …the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 64, on great things growing from small beginnings ("li" is a Chinese measure of distance).

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 9, on knowing when to stop.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 23, on speaking little, since even heaven and earth cannot keep up violence for long.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 24, on self-display and overreaching.

entries.name: Laozi
entries.en: Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
entries.work: The Tao Teh King, or the Tao and its Characteristics
entries.context: The Tao Teh King, chapter 15, on the old masters of the Way.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: The great man is he who does not lose his child's heart.
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF THOSE OTHERS, THEY ARE NOT TO BE, chapter XII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book IV, Part II, chapter 12.

entries.name: Mencius
entries.en: …when Heaven is about to confer a great office on any one, it first exercises his mind with suffering, and his sinews and bones with toil
entries.work: The Life and Works of Mencius
entries.locator: OF SEVERAL EMINENT WORTHIES OF FORMER TIMES, Book VII
entries.context: The Works of Mencius, Book VI, Part II, chapter 15, on the hardships that came before great figures of antiquity took office.

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: Death is nothing to us; for that which is dissolved is devoid of sensation, and that which is devoid of sensation is nothing to us.
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, number 2, as preserved by Diogenes Laertius.

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: It is not possible to live pleasantly without living prudently, and honourably, and justly
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, number 5, on pleasure and virtue being inseparable.

entries.name: Epicurus
entries.en: Of all the things which wisdom provides for the happiness of the whole life, by far the most important is the acquisition of friendship.
entries.work: The Life of Epicurus, the Letters to Herodotus and Pythocles, and the Principal Doctrines
entries.context: Epicurus's Principal Doctrines, on friendship (numbered 28 in this edition).

entries.name: Karl Marx
entries.en: The history of all hitherto existing societies is the history of class struggles.
entries.work: The Communist Manifesto
entries.context: The opening sentence of the first section of The Communist Manifesto, by Marx and Engels.

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: …by doing just actions we come to be just; by doing the actions of self-mastery we come to be perfected in self-mastery; and by doing brave actions brave.
entries.work: The Nicomachean Ethics
entries.context: The Nicomachean Ethics, Book II, chapter 1: virtues are formed by practice, as skills are.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: …the unexamined life is not worth living
entries.work: Apology
entries.context: Plato's Apology, Socrates at his trial, explaining why he cannot stop examining himself and others.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: …be of good cheer about death, and know of a certainty, that no evil can happen to a good man, either in life or after death.
entries.work: Apology
entries.context: Plato's Apology, Socrates' last words to the judges who voted to acquit him.

entries.name: Plato
entries.en: …the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing
entries.work: The Republic
entries.context: Plato's Republic, Book II, Socrates on the education of the young.

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Enchiridion of Epictetus, section 5.

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Of things some are in our power, and others are not.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The opening words of the Enchiridion of Epictetus.

entries.name: Epictetus
entries.en: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it.
entries.work: A Selection from the Discourses of Epictetus, with the Enchiridion
entries.context: The Enchiridion of Epictetus, section 11, on loss as returning what was lent.

entries.name: Niccolo Machiavelli
entries.en: Every one sees what you appear to be, few really know what you are
entries.work: The Prince
entries.locator: OF THE ART OF WAR, CHAPTER XVIII
entries.context: The Prince, chapter XVIII, on appearance and reality in a ruler's reputation.

entries.name: Rene Descartes
entries.en: Good sense is, of all things among men, the most equally distributed
entries.work: Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences
entries.context: The opening sentence of Descartes' Discourse on Method; it goes on to note that no one wishes for more of it than they have.

entries.name: Rene Descartes
entries.en: …to divide each of the difficulties under examination into as many parts as possible, and as might be necessary for its adequate solution.
entries.work: Discourse on the Method of Rightly Conducting One's Reason and of Seeking Truth in the Sciences
entries.context: Discourse on Method, Part II: the second of the four rules Descartes set himself.

entries.name: Aristotle
entries.en: …it is not one swallow or one fine day that makes a spring, so it is not one day or a short time that makes a man blessed and happy.
entries.work: The Nicomachean Ethics
entries.context: The Nicomachean Ethics, Book I, chapter 7: happiness belongs to a whole life, not a single day.

entries.name: George Berkeley
entries.en: …we have first raised a dust and then complain we cannot see.
entries.work: A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge
entries.context: Berkeley's introduction to A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge, on difficulties philosophers make for themselves.

entries.name: George Berkeley
entries.en: Few men think; yet all have opinions.
entries.work: Three Dialogues Between Hylas and Philonous
entries.context: Three Dialogues between Hylas and Philonous; Philonous, Berkeley's spokesman, answers Hylas.

entries.name: Ralph Waldo Emerson
entries.en: Nothing can bring you peace but yourself.
entries.work: Essays: First Series
entries.context: The second-to-last line of Emerson's essay "Self-Reliance", warning against trusting good luck for peace of mind.
